transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-16
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood, AE); Priya Shah (Redwood, SE); Liam O'Connor (RidgePay, Eng Mgr); Sana Rahman (RidgePay, Lead ML); Oliver Chen (RidgePay, DevOps)

Summary:
Quick SDK walkthrough for Python and TypeScript quickstarts, cover auth & env setup, demo a simple text-generation call, streaming example, and notes on Dedicated vs Hosted and Optimize recommendations. Agree next steps to run a small benchmark and share security docs.

Topics:
- SDK install (pip/npm)
- API key / env var setup / KMS mention
- Quickstart examples (Python + TS)
- Streaming vs non-streaming, callbacks
- Auth patterns for server vs client
- Dedicated / Private options and network requirements
- Optimize: batching, KV/prefix caching, quantization suggestions

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan, AE on the RidgePay account, and Priya's going to lead the SDK walkthrough. How are we doing?
[00:10] Liam O'Connor: Good, thanks. We are excited, want to get our engineers up to speed.
[00:14] Sana Rahman: Yep hi all. We mainly care about throughput and keeping latency under 200ms for the customer-facing flows.
[00:20] Priya Shah: Great, quick agenda: install the SDKs, set API key, run Python quickstart, show TypeScript example, streaming, and then a few production notes - auth, env, and Optimize tips.
[00:30] Oliver Chen: Sweet. We'll be looking at both hosted and if that doesn't meet our residency needs maybe Dedicated or Private.
[00:36] Priya Shah: Perfect. Okay first step, pip and npm installs. For Python: pip install redwood-inference (note: the package name is redwood-inference). For TypeScript: npm install @redwood/inference-sdk or yarn add @redwood/inference-sdk. Sometimes the auto transcript shows slightly different package names, but that's the correct one.
[00:54] Liam O'Connor: Do you have a one-liner to create a venv and run? We usually standardize on venv in RidgePay.
[01:00] Priya Shah: Totally. python -m venv venv; source venv/bin/activate; pip install redwood-inference. Then export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk_live_xxx or put in .env. We also have a starter repo with a .env.example.
[01:12] Sana Rahman: Where do we get the API key? Is that from the Console?
[01:16] Jordan Kim: Yes, I'll provision a trial key for you and drop it in Slack. The Console -> API Keys, create service key, restrict by route if you want.
[01:24] Oliver Chen: Can we do KMS-backed keys? We use customer-managed keys in KMS for secrets.
[01:28] Priya Shah: For Private deployments we support KMS/HSM integrations; for Hosted we encrypt keys at rest and can do customer-managed keys via enterprise support - I'll include the docs.
[01:38] Liam O'Connor: Great. Walkthrough, please.
[01:42] Priya Shah: Ok Python quickstart. Code snippet: from redwood import RedwoodClient; client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.environ['REDWOOD_API_KEY']); resp = client.generate(model='redwood-llm-2', prompt='Summarize payment flow'); print(resp.text). That's simplified - real code includes timeout, retries, and streaming handlers.
[02:00] Sana Rahman: Quick Q: model names - redwood-llm-2, redwood-instruct, are those real?
[02:05] Priya Shah: Yes we have a model catalog in the Console. Names may vary, sometimes transcript swaps hyphens. We'll share the current catalog.
[02:12] Jordan Kim: Also you can pin model versions for consistent behavior in production.
[02:16] Priya Shah: For TypeScript the snippet looks like: import { Redwood } from '@redwood/inference-sdk'; const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); const resp = await client.generate({ model: 'redwood-llm-2', prompt: '...' }); console.log(resp.output);
[02:34] Oliver Chen: Do you expose streaming via SSE or websockets?
[02:38] Priya Shah: We support streaming over HTTP using chunked responses and common SDK callbacks, and also WebSocket tool calling in some SDKs. Example: client.stream({ ... }, (chunk) => { process.stdout.write(chunk); }). For TS the SDK returns an async iterator in one of the helpers.
[02:54] Liam O'Connor: Good. We'll need examples of aborting streams and reconnect logic.
[02:58] Priya Shah: Yep we'll include those patterns - backpressure, reconnect with last token id, etc.
[03:06] Sana Rahman: How do we handle auth for browser vs server? We can't leak the service key client-side.
[03:10] Priya Shah: Best practice: keep the service key on the server; create short-lived session tokens via your backend if you need client-side streaming. We also support signed URLs and ephemeral keys via the Console or API.
[03:20] Liam O'Connor: Any built-in RBAC or SSO integrations for who can create keys?
[03:24] Jordan Kim: Yes Console supports SSO (SAML/OIDC), RBAC with roles, and audit logs. We'll share the admin docs in the follow-up.
[03:34] Oliver Chen: Ok network stuff: for Private deployment we need list of CIDRs and ports.
[03:38] Priya Shah: For Private/VPC we provide a network requirements doc - typical ports 443 outbound, plus we can run in your VPC with peering. Oliver, I'll flag you in the doc.
[03:48] Liam O'Connor: Sounds good. Next, Optimize recommendations - Priya?
[03:52] Priya Shah: Sure. Optimize has three levers: batching, KV/prefix caching, and quantization/model selection. For high-throughput endpoints, enable continuous batching with appropriate latency SLOs. If you have heavy prefix reuse (like standard prompts), KV caching saves a lot. For less-critical latency but big cost savings consider an int8 quantized variant.
[04:12] Sana Rahman: How do we control batching in the SDK?
[04:15] Priya Shah: In the SDK you set the route and the batching policy on the server side in the Console or via the Dedicated config. Example: route.batch.max_tokens and route.batch.max_latency_ms. The SDK just hits the route, the runtime handles batching.
[04:26] Jordan Kim: We can demo a small benchmark comparing latency/cost between hosted and a dedicated pool next week.
[04:32] Liam O'Connor: That'd be helpful.
[04:34] Priya Shah: Back to code, small more realistic Python example with streaming and chunk handling:
[04:38] [screen share audible - code reading]
from redwood import RedwoodClient
client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.environ.get('REDWOOD_API_KEY'), timeout=30)
async for chunk in client.stream_generate(model='redwood-llm-2', prompt='Explain the 3-step payment auth flow'):
    # chunk may include partial tokens
    print(chunk.text, end='')

[04:57] Sana Rahman: The streaming example is good. Are there built-in retry policies?
[05:01] Priya Shah: SDK has configurable retry/backoff; we recommend idempotency keys for non-idempotent operations if you want dedup.
[05:07] Oliver Chen: About logs - do we get request-level tracing?
[05:11] Jordan Kim: Console provides per-request traces, token breakdowns, and we export logs to your S3/BigQuery for long-term retention if needed.
[05:18] Liam O'Connor: Is there a way to pass user IDs and get cost/latency broken down by user?
[05:22] Priya Shah: Yes add metadata fields like client_user_id and group_id; they show up in the Console for filtering. We'll show the dashboard in the follow-up demo.
[05:32] Sana Rahman: Any gotchas with TypeScript typings?
[05:35] Priya Shah: There are TS types in the npm package; for custom tooling you may want to extend the type defs - we'll include the snippet in the repo. Occasionally the auto-generated types are slightly off for newer model responses, but we keep them updated.
[05:48] Liam O'Connor: Let's cover quickstart repos.
[05:50] Priya Shah: We have a starter repo with two folders: python-quickstart and ts-quickstart, includes Dockerfile for server, examples for streaming, and a sample infra.tf for Dedicated/private. Link: github.com/redwood-inference/starter-quickstarts (we'll post exact link).
[06:06] Oliver Chen: Great. For CICD how do we rotate keys?
[06:09] Jordan Kim: Use short-lived service accounts or Vault/KMS integration. For Hosted you can generate limited-scope keys and rotate regularly. For Private, you can store keys in your own secret manager.
[06:18] Sana Rahman: Are there SDK examples for batching multiple prompts in one request?
[06:22] Priya Shah: Yes, you send an array of prompts to client.generateBatch([...]) and the runtime will group them into batches. When ordering matters you can request deterministic ordering and a merge strategy.
[06:31] Liam O'Connor: We may want to run a POC with 100 req/s. Will Dedicated handle that?
[06:36] Priya Shah: Dedicated pools are for predictable throughput; you reserve GPU capacity and set autoscale policies. We'll size a pool for expected RPS - Priya to prepare sizing recommendation based on your sample workload.
[06:47] Oliver Chen: Any enterprise network compliance like SOC2/ISO?
[06:50] Jordan Kim: Yes, SOC 2 and ISO-27001, plus detailed audit logs; we'll attach the compliance pack.
[06:58] [pause - background noise, someone typing]
[07:04] Priya Shah: Quick note on function calling / tool calling. If your app integrates with internal systems we support structured function outputs and tool calling so the model returns structured JSON and you can wire that into downstream calls.
[07:18] Sana Rahman: That might help reduce hallucinations if we validate outputs.
[07:21] Priya Shah: Exactly. We'll include the function signature examples in the repo.
[07:28] Liam O'Connor: What about rate limits and quotas?
[07:31] Jordan Kim: Hosted plans have per-account quotas and rate limits; Dedicated has capacity-based limits. We can also set per-route quotas for internal control.
[07:41] Oliver Chen: Can we set traffic-splitting for canary releases?
[07:44] Priya Shah: Yes Console supports canary rollouts, percentage traffic, and automatic fallback to a baseline model if the canary fails.
[07:52] Liam O'Connor: We'll need rollback procedures documented.
[07:55] Jordan Kim: We'll include runbooks for rollbacks and incident response.
[08:00] Priya Shah: Now I'll demo a short live run - simple prompt to show live tokens. (typing sounds)
[08:08] [short pause - network audio slight stutter]
[08:12] Priya Shah: Ok here's a streaming run, you'll see token chunks arriving. (demo) You can abort with ctrl-c or send cancel via the SDK's cancel token.
[08:24] Sana Rahman: Looks smooth.
[08:26] Priya Shah: For perf tuning, measure p50/p95 latency and token-per-second costs. The SDK emits timings and token counts in headers for each response.
[08:37] Liam O'Connor: Any SDK support for retry-after header when overloaded?
[08:40] Priya Shah: Yes we return standard 429 with Retry-After; SDK has built-in respect for Retry-After and exponential backoff.
[08:48] Oliver Chen: About data retention and logs, do you persist prompts?
[08:52] Jordan Kim: By default Hosted stores logs for 30 days for observability; enterprise customers can opt out or set retention. Private you fully control retention. We'll share the data handling policy.
[09:04] Sana Rahman: Good to know.
[09:08] Priya Shah: Final quick items: sample infra for Dedicated includes terraform modules for autoscaling policies and GPU types (A100, H100, etc.) - we'll share recommended instances for low-latency gen. Also quantized models are cheaper; we can show quality regressions vs base in the benchmark.
[09:28] Liam O'Connor: For the benchmark next week we'll provide sample prompts and traffic pattern.
[09:33] Jordan Kim: Great. I'll send the starter repo + pricing spreadsheet + SOC2 docs after the call.
[09:39] Oliver Chen: Can you include an example of ephemeral keys flow for browser streaming?
[09:43] Priya Shah: Yes, that's in the quickstart under ts-quickstart/client-ephemeral-token.md.
[09:49] Sana Rahman: Any limitations on max tokens or window sizes?
[09:53] Priya Shah: We support up to several thousand tokens depending on the model variant; the Console shows sequence length limits per model. Longer contexts may affect latency.
[10:02] Liam O'Connor: Alright let's recap next steps.
[10:05] Jordan Kim: Recap: Jordan to provision trial API key and share repo and docs; Priya to prepare benchmark config and sizing guidance; Oliver to share network/CIDR details; schedule follow-up SE-led benchmark week of 2/23. Anything else?
